text: Lesson 21 covered the pieces — command groups, output formats, query filtering. This lesson strings them together into what an administrator actually does: stand up a resource group, create a real resource inside it, confirm what's really there, then tear the whole thing down.

Four steps, four real commands, no simplified stand-ins. az group create makes the container, first. az vm create provisions the actual resource inside it. az resource list confirms what's really there, every type, not just the one you created. az group delete removes all of it, in one call.

az group create makes the container. az vm create, with an image alias like Ubuntu2204, an admin username, generate-ssh-keys for authentication instead of a password, and a size like Standard_B1s, provisions the actual virtual machine. One command does everything the multi-screen Portal wizard does: picks the image, provisions the disk, configures networking defaults, and sets up SSH access.

Here's a gap beginners hit: az vm list only shows VMs, but a resource group usually holds more — the VM's managed disk, its network interface, its public IP, the VNet it's attached to. az resource list shows all of them, regardless of type. Run it against rg-cli-demo and you get five or six resource types back, all created as side effects of that one az vm create call.

Cleanup could mean deleting the VM, then its disk, then its NIC, then its public IP, one command at a time. Nobody does that. az group delete, with --yes to skip the confirmation prompt and --no-wait to return your terminal immediately, removes everything inside the group in a single call. The resource group isn't just an organizational folder — it's the one blast-radius boundary that makes full cleanup one command instead of a scavenger hunt.

That's the full CLI lifecycle: create the group, create the resource, confirm with az resource list, delete the group when you're done. Next: the same four tasks, but through Azure PowerShell's Az module and its Verb-Noun cmdlets instead of the az CLI.
